extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic plays: how to construct plot, incidents, recognition, character, and staging to produce pity and fear. Draws on classical Aristotelian rules and examples (Oedipus, Medea, Iphigenia, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot parts (reversal, recognition, tragic incident)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two parts of the Plot—Reversal and Recognition—turn upon surprises. A third part is the Tragic Incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis) are central and hinge on surprise. The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, etc.). These three operate together to create the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of Tragedy (prologue, episode, exodos, choric song)
rubrics_metrics.description: The separate parts into which Tragedy is divided are Prologue, Episode, Exodos, Choric song (the Parodos and the Stasimon), with occasional stage-actor songs and Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Prologos precedes the Parodos; the Episode lies between complete choric songs; the Exodos has no choric song after it. Parodos is the Chorus's first undivided utterance; Stasimon is a choral ode without anapaests or trochees; Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors. These parts must be treated as elements of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex over simple plot construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots allow for the interplay of reversal and recognition and create the distinctive tragic effects (pity and fear). Simple plots lack the same tragic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate actions that excite pity and fear (distinctive aim of Tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should imitate actions which excite pity and fear; this is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet must aim to produce the pleasure proper to Tragedy — that which comes from pity and fear through imitation — not other pleasures. Incidents should be constructed to arouse these emotions (e.g., Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitable moral status of the protagonist (hamartia principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune must not be the spectacle of a virtuous man nor the downfall of an utter villain; rather, the protagonist should be between these extremes: not eminently good and just, nor wholly bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The misfortune should be brought about not by vice or depravity but by some error or frailty (hamartia) in a character renowned and prosperous (brought from prosperity to adversity). A virtuous man's fall shocks without pity or fear; the villain's fall arouses neither pity nor fear. Examples: Oedipus, Thyestes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune should be from good to bad and caused by error, not vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be from good to bad (prosperity to adversity) and should come about as the result not of vice, but of some great error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (misfortune of a man like ourselves). Plays where bad → good or villain → misfortune fail to produce the proper tragic responses. Euripides's unhappy endings follow this right principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of issue: prefer single-threaded plots
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue, rather than double as some maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-threaded plots (like Odyssey-type double threads with opposite catastrophes) cater to spectator weakness and produce a pleasure nearer to comedy; the true tragic pleasure is served by a single coherent catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arouse pity/fear by plot-structure rather than spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way, and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, the hearer will thrill with horror and melt to pity. Reliance on spectacle to create the monstrous rather than the terrible is a sign of defective art. Spectacle is a concomitant, not the essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose incidents among relations (friends, enemies, kinsfolk) to maximize pity/fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of tragic effect must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; but the strongest effects occur between those who are near or dear (kinship or friendship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to look for: brother killing brother, son killing father, mother killing son, etc. If the tragic incident involves strangers or mere enemies, it arouses little pity except for suffering itself. Use family/friend ties to intensify emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle traditional (received) legends with invention and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may not destroy the framework of the received legends but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve essential received facts (e.g., Clytemnestra slain by Orestes) while inventing and managing the details well. The poet should explain what 'handle well' means by showing skilful arrangement and novelty within tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the deed-perpetrated-in-ignorance-with-later-recognition arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Horrible deeds may occur knowingly, unknowingly with later recognition, or be about to be done and then recognized; of these the best is that the deed should be perpetrated in ignorance and the discovery made afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking: (worst) about to act knowing the persons and then not acting (shocking without being tragic) → (better) deed perpetrated knowingly → (best) deed done in ignorance with later discovery producing a startling, tragic effect. Examples: Medea (knows), Oedipus (ignorant then recognition), Cresphontes/Merope (recognition before deed saves life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character virtues: goodness is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at. First, and most important, it must be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be expressive of character; a character is good if the purpose is good. 'Good' is relative to class (a woman or a slave may be good in their class).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character propriety (appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second aim: propriety — character traits must be appropriate to the sex, station, and role (e.g., manly valour is not fitting as a general trait in a woman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a type of manly valour, but for a woman to be valiant or terrible would be inapposite. Choose traits fitting to the character's social/biological role to maintain plausibility and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character truth to life (probability/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third aim: character must be true to life; actions and speeches must follow by the rule either of necessity or of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person of given character should speak or act in ways that are necessary or probable. The poet should always aim at the necessary or the probable in both structure and characterization so events feel natural and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency (even inconsistent characters must be consistently inconsistent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth aim: consistency — even if the model being imitated is inconsistent, the character presented must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous badness, indecorousness, or sudden unexplained changes (examples: Menelaus in Orestes as gratuitously bad; Iphigenia at Aulis as inconsistent). Maintain an internally coherent pattern of behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: The unravelling/complication must arise from the plot itself; avoid Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling no less than the complication must arise out of the plot itself; it must not be brought about by the Deus ex Machina,—except for events external to the drama (antecedent/subsequent events beyond human knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deus ex Machina may be employed only for events outside the drama (things ascribed to the gods). Within the action, nothing irrational should occur; irrational elements, if unavoidable, should lie outside the tragic action (e.g., aspects of Oedipus explained as outside the drama). Examples of bad use: Medea and the Return of the Greeks in the Iliad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — prefer recognitions arising from incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition types are ranked: by signs (congenital or acquired), by tokens, by poet-invented speech (bad), by memory, by reasoning, and best of all—recognition arising naturally from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congenital signs (birthmarks, traits) and acquired bodily marks (scars), external tokens (necklaces, letters) are usable but allow degrees of skill. Poet-invented recognitions (character says what the poet wants rather than the plot requiring it) are faulty. Best recognitions are natural turns of incident (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia). Reasoning-based and memory-based recognitions are intermediate in artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recognitions proved solely by formal tokens or artificial proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of tokens for the express purpose of proof—and any formal proof with or without tokens—is a less artistic mode of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better is a recognition produced by the turn of incident (e.g., 'bath scene' in the Odyssey) or by natural causes in the plot. Poet-invented revelations (characters telling rather than plot revealing) are allied to this fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the scene vividly before the writer's eyes (vividness, staging, gesture)
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing everything vividly (as if a spectator) helps discover what is in keeping and avoid inconsistencies. Work the play out with appropriate gestures; emotions are most convincing when expressed strongly and truly. Episodes should be brief within the drama and fitted organically to the plot (examples: Iphigenia's absences, the madness and recovery in Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrationality within the action; if irrational, keep it outside the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the action there must be nothing irrational. If the irrational cannot be excluded, it should be outside the scope of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational elements inside the drama offend the audience's sense of plausibility (example: irrational parts of the Oedipus story are excused by being outside the tragic action). Ensure cause-and-effect logic governs events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture: imitate types but ennoble them (like good portrait-painters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy imitates persons above the common level, the example of good portrait-painters should be followed: reproduce distinctive form of the original while making a likeness true to life and yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should preserve the type and yet ennoble it. When representing irascible or indolent characters, keep the type recognizable but rendered in an elevated way (examples: Achilles as portrayed by Agathon and Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory appeals and spectacle as concomitants, not the essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not neglect appeals to the senses (spectacle, visual effects), which, though not among the essentials, are concomitants of poetry; there is much room for error here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can aid but should not substitute for the plotted incidents that produce pity and fear. Overreliance on producing the monstrous visually is a defect; aim the sensory elements to support, not override, the plot and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose by sketching general outline first, then fill episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes the story ready-made or constructs it himself, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the overall plot and then compose episodes that are short, appropriate, and organically connected (episodes should be consonant with the main action and contribute to the recognition and catastrophe rather than distract).
